module_title: Legislative Procedures, Ordinance Making, and Veto Powers
introduction: This intermediate tier transitions to the actual mechanics of constitutional powers. It breaks down how a Bill becomes a Law, the exceptional legislative powers of the Executive (Ordinances), and the Pardoning and Veto powers.

core_concepts.title: Money Bills vs. Ordinary Bills
core_concepts.description:
- Ordinary Bill: Can be introduced in either House. Requires a simple majority. Deadlocks are resolved by a Joint Sitting (Art 108).
- Money Bill (Article 110): Deals strictly with taxation, borrowing, or the Consolidated Fund of India. 
  * Rules: Can ONLY be introduced in the Lok Sabha with the prior recommendation of the President. The Rajya Sabha has no power to reject or amend it (can only delay it for 14 days). The Speaker of the Lok Sabha has the final authority to certify whether a bill is a Money Bill.

core_concepts.title: Ordinance Making Power (Arts 123 & 213)
core_concepts.description:
The Constitution grants the Executive the power to make laws when the Legislature is not in session to deal with urgent matters.
- President (Art 123) / Governor (Art 213).
- Validity: An ordinance has the exact same force as an Act of Parliament. However, it must be approved by the Legislature within **6 weeks** from its reassembly. Maximum possible life of an ordinance is 6 months + 6 weeks.

core_concepts.title: Veto Powers of the President
core_concepts.description:
When a bill is sent for assent (Art 111), the President has three vetos:
1. Absolute Veto: Withholding assent completely (usually applied to private member bills or if the cabinet resigns).
2. Suspensive Veto: Returning the bill for reconsideration. However, if Parliament passes it again (with or without amendments), the President MUST give assent.
3. Pocket Veto: Neither ratifying nor rejecting nor returning the bill, simply keeping it pending indefinitely (because the Constitution prescribes no time limit for the President to act).

core_concepts.title: Pardoning Power: President vs. Governor
core_concepts.description:
- President (Art 72): Can pardon sentences for Union laws, Court-Martial (military courts), and **Death Sentences**.
- Governor (Art 161): Can pardon sentences for State laws. However, a Governor CANNOT pardon a death sentence (can only suspend, remit, or commute it) and has no power over court-martial sentences.

important_entities.name: Joint Sitting (Article 108)
important_entities.key_fact: A mechanism to resolve deadlocks between the two Houses.
important_entities.significance: Summoned by the President, but **Presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha** (a highly tested fact). It is applicable only to Ordinary Bills and Financial Bills, NEVER to Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will ask: 'Can the President use a pocket veto on a Constitutional Amendment Bill?' The answer is **NO**. The 24th Amendment Act (1971) made it obligatory for the President to give his assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Absolute = No, Suspensive = Try Again, Pocket = Ignore
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Absolute kills the bill. Suspensive bounces it back. Pocket puts it in cold storage.

exam_strategy_tips: If a Judiciary exam asks 'Who decides whether a particular bill is a Money Bill or not?', unconditionally select **The Speaker of the Lok Sabha**.
